inference.explanation: Spikes are timed to the valve closure, grow toward the dead end, breaks cluster there, pipe walls are sound, and slowing the valve cuts the spikes. Station overpressure would appear system wide, and soil attack would thin walls that repairs find sound.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Require slow closing or surge protection on the user connection and add transient logging to the street after the fix
Renew the last 200 m with heavier pipe and leave the valve as is
Remove the industrial user from the system

nextClue.explanation: Controlling the transient at its source protects the whole street, and logging verifies the fix under real operations.

clueText.nc-a: After the valve change, dead end spikes stay below 600 kPa and no breaks occur the following year.
clueText.nc-b: Heavier pipe still faces daily hammer that will find the next weakest point.
clueText.nc-c: Removing a customer is disproportionate when a valve change removes the cause.

tasks.prompt: Acoustic loggers deployed across an Alberta district hear strong noise at two points 400 m apart on the same main, but correlation between them will not settle on a single leak position.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional district in a Leduc area system. Crews ground microphone surveyed the full length after the failed correlation.

evidence.label: Ground microphone survey finds noise peaks at two separate spots, each sharp and local.
Step testing drops flow in two distinct steps as each of the two spots is isolated in turn.
Each spot, excavated in turn, reveals its own leak: a service leak at one and a joint leak at the other.
Night flow falls by about half after the first repair and to baseline after the second.
Pipe between the two spots is quiet on the ground survey.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: One leak is moving along the main between surveys
The correlation equipment is faulty and there is only one leak
Both noise peaks are echoes of a single leak at the midpoint
Two separate leaks on the same main confused the correlation, and both had to be repaired to clear the district loss

inference.explanation: Two sharp local peaks, two distinct step drops, two leaks found at excavation, and flow falling in two stages after two repairs prove two sources. Echoes and equipment faults cannot produce two physical leaks at two digs.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Continue correlating between the two points until it settles
Close the district case only after a post repair night flow confirms baseline, and keep both logger points in the watch list for a month
Repair the louder leak and assume the second peak was an echo

nextClue.explanation: Post repair night flow is the acceptance test for the whole district, not for any single dig.

clueText.nc-a: Correlation between two real leaks will keep failing for a physical reason, not an equipment one.
clueText.nc-b: Baseline night flow confirms both leaks are cleared, and the watch list catches any early recurrence.
clueText.nc-c: The second peak was a real service leak that would have kept losing water.

tasks.prompt: A Saskatchewan zone fed by two reducing stations from opposite ends shows a low pressure pocket exactly between them that neither station adjustment cures.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone in a Regina area system. Crews logged pressures at both stations and at the pocket over a week of trials.

evidence.label: Both stations hold their setpoints at their outlets all week.
Pocket pressure falls at peak and recovers at night, with the drop growing with zone flow.
A normally open valve on the mid zone main between the stations is found closed, forcing the pocket to be fed the long way from both ends.
Opening the mid zone valve in a trial lifts pocket peak pressure to normal at once.
No leaks or breaks are found in the pocket during the week.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The closed mid zone valve forces long feed paths, so friction loss at peak starves the pocket between the stations
Both reducing stations are undersized for the zone
The pocket sits on a hidden hill higher than both stations
Pocket customers all use water in the same peak pattern

inference.explanation: Both stations prove their setpoints, the pattern tracks flow like friction loss, and opening one mid zone valve cures it instantly. A hidden hill would lower pocket pressure at night too, and station size cannot explain a cure from a valve position.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Raise both station setpoints until the pocket is satisfied
Install a third reducing station at the pocket
Leave the mid zone valve open, tag it as a critical normally open valve, and add it to the zone valve audit list

nextClue.explanation: Tagging critical valves from real incidents keeps the zone audit focused on positions that can starve a pocket.

clueText.nc-a: Higher setpoints would overpressure streets near both stations to serve a friction problem.
clueText.nc-b: A third station adds cost to work around one closed valve.
clueText.nc-c: The pocket holds normal peak pressure for the month after the audit listing.

tasks.prompt: Free chlorine samples in a Manitoba zone read low every Monday morning and normal by Tuesday, in a pattern tied to a small storage tank that sits idle over weekends.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone in a Dauphin area system with a small tank on a weekday industrial feed. Tank level and zone sampling records cover six weeks.

evidence.label: The tank level does not move from Friday evening to Monday morning in any of the six weeks.
Monday zone samples near the tank read 0.08 mg/L, while samples far from the tank read 0.5 mg/L the same mornings.
By Tuesday, after weekday demand cycles the tank, near tank samples recover to normal.
Plant and zone entry residuals are steady all week.
Flushing near the tank on a Monday trial restores its samples the same day.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant underdoses every weekend and recovers on weekdays
Water standing in the idle tank over the weekend loses its residual and slugs the nearby zone each Monday
Monday samples are mishandled after the weekend break
Weekend demand in the zone is so high it strips residual

inference.explanation: Entry residual is steady, only near tank samples fall, the tank is proven idle all weekend, and cycling or flushing restores them on schedule. Mishandled samples would not recover in step with tank cycling, and high weekend demand contradicts an idle tank level.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Programme a small weekend exchange for the tank and add a Monday residual check near it to the sampling round
Raise the plant weekend dose for the whole system
Move the Monday samples to Tuesdays permanently

nextClue.explanation: A programmed exchange keeps tank water fresh through its idle period, which is the proven cause window.

clueText.nc-a: Monday near tank samples hold above 0.4 mg/L in the weeks after the exchange begins.
clueText.nc-b: System wide dosing treats water that already tests normal far from the tank.
clueText.nc-c: Moving samples hides the one morning the zone is actually at risk.

tasks.prompt: An Alberta reservoir inspection programme finds one tank with a failed coating and early steel corrosion, while sister tanks of the same age are in good condition.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional fleet comparison in a Camrose area system. All tanks were built in the same programme year with the same coating specification.

evidence.label: The failed tank held raw well water with high dissolved oxygen for its first five years before a treatment change, unlike its sisters.
Coating failure maps to the waterline band where wet and dry cycling was greatest in those years.
Sister tanks that always held treated water show sound coating at the same age.
Steel thickness at the failed band is measurably reduced, while sister tank readings are at specification.
Water quality from the failed tank shows occasional iron colour after level changes stir the band.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: All tanks from that programme year will fail the same way this year
The coating applicator used a bad batch on every tank
The early years of aggressive raw water service destroyed this tank coating, so its condition is a service history effect, not a fleet age effect
The failed tank is simply the oldest and the others will match it soon

inference.explanation: Only the raw water tank failed, its damage maps to its unique service band, and sisters with the same coating and age are sound. A bad batch or pure age effect would appear across the fleet, which inspection disproves.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Recoat the entire fleet this year as a precaution
Bring this tank forward for recoating and steel repair, and set sister tank inspections on their own condition based interval
Take the failed tank out of service permanently without repair assessment

nextClue.explanation: Condition based scheduling spends first where measured steel loss exists and keeps sound tanks in service.

clueText.nc-a: Fleet wide recoating spends on tanks proven sound by the same inspection programme.
clueText.nc-b: The repair scope is set from the thickness survey, and sisters stay on their normal inspection cycle.
clueText.nc-c: Permanent removal loses storage the zone needs when a scoped repair can restore it.

tasks.prompt: A Saskatchewan station energy audit finds one pump using far more energy per volume than its identical partner, though both deliver the same duty point.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional duplex station in a Humboldt area system with per pump energy metering added for the audit. Both pumps were tested at the same flow and head.

evidence.label: At the matched test point, Pump A uses 0.21 kWh per cubic metre and Pump B uses 0.31.
Pump B suction strainer is found half blocked with scale flakes, raising its suction loss.
Pump B discharge pressure must run higher to hold the same duty flow against the added suction loss and a partly fouled check.
Cleaning the strainer and check in a trial brings Pump B energy per volume close to Pump A.
Motor electrical tests on both pumps are normal and equal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Pump B motor is electrically inferior to Pump A
The energy meter on Pump B over reads by half
Pump B impeller is a different size from Pump A
Added suction and check losses on Pump B force it to work harder for the same duty, wasting energy

inference.explanation: Motors test equal, the losses are found physically on Pump B suction and check, and cleaning them restores its energy figure in a live trial. A meter error would not change with cleaning, and impeller size would not respond to strainer work.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace Pump B motor with a premium efficiency model
Run Pump A alone and retire Pump B
Add strainer and check condition to the station efficiency round and trend energy per volume per pump monthly

nextClue.explanation: Per pump energy trending catches creeping hydraulic losses while they are still cheap cleaning jobs.

clueText.nc-a: The motor tested equal to its partner, so replacement buys nothing.
clueText.nc-b: Retiring a needed standby pump for a strainer cleaning issue weakens station reliability.
clueText.nc-c: Pump B holds its recovered efficiency for the next quarter under the new round.

tasks.prompt: A British Columbia arena and pool complex passes its backflow device tests, yet the utility survey finds its highest hazard, a chemical feed room, connected ahead of every device on the service.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional complex in a Vernon area system. The survey traced every branch from the service entrance with building staff.

evidence.label: Two testable assemblies protect the pool and arena branches and both pass current tests.
The chemical feed room branch tees off the main service line before either assembly.
Chemical feed pumps in that room pressurize treatment lines above street pressure.
No device of any kind is fitted on the chemical room branch.
Building drawings on file with the utility show the tee, so the gap is visible in the survey records.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The chemical room is an unprotected high hazard branch despite the passing tests on other branches
Passing device tests mean the whole complex is protected
The chemical room is low hazard because it is small
The tee location does not matter as long as devices exist somewhere

inference.explanation: Protection applies branch by branch: the pressurized chemical branch has no device at all, while the passing devices guard different branches. Test paperwork for other lines cannot protect a tee that bypasses them, and pressurized chemical feed is a high hazard by its nature.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Require a testable assembly on the chemical room branch and update the survey record to show protection by branch
File the survey as satisfactory because two devices passed
Ask the complex to keep chemical pressures low by procedure

nextClue.explanation: Branch level survey records prevent a passing average from hiding an unprotected hazard again.

clueText.nc-a: The new branch assembly passes its first test and the survey record now maps all three branches.
clueText.nc-b: Filing as satisfactory would certify a gap the survey itself documented.
clueText.nc-c: Procedural pressure limits are not a substitute for a testable device on a high hazard branch.

tasks.prompt: A northern Alberta utility compares two winters: breaks rose in the colder winter, but only on mains installed in shallow trenches shared with other utilities.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional comparison in a Fort McMurray area system. Trench records show shared trench sections were backfilled with native frozen material in one construction era.

evidence.label: Shared trench sections account for most of the extra breaks in the colder winter.
Solo trench mains of the same age and depth nearby show little change between the winters.
Break excavations on shared sections find voids and uneven support from the poor backfill.
Pressures and transient records are similar in both winters.
Failure types on shared sections are beam and circumferential breaks consistent with uneven support under frost load.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Shared trench mains are older and simply at end of life
Poor shared trench backfill leaves those mains unevenly supported, so deep frost loading breaks them preferentially
Other utilities are leaking heat or water that damages the mains
The colder winter raised system pressure and broke the weakest pipes

inference.explanation: Same age solo trench mains nearby are largely unaffected, excavations show the support defect, failure types match uneven support, and pressures match between winters. Age alone cannot select trench type, and no heat or water damage is reported at the excavations.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace all mains of that age regardless of trench type
Target shared trench sections for support assessment in the renewal programme and specify controlled backfill on all future shared trenches
Lower winter system pressure across the utility

nextClue.explanation: Trench based targeting focuses renewal on the support defect the evidence isolates, and the backfill specification stops its recurrence.

clueText.nc-a: Age based replacement would renew sound solo trench mains while the defect is in support, not age.
clueText.nc-b: The renewal list ranks shared trench sections first, with solo trench sections of the same age deferred on condition.
clueText.nc-c: Pressure was the same in both winters, so it cannot explain the difference between them.

tasks.prompt: A flushing programme in a Saskatchewan city cleans most zones well, but turbidity at one zone hydrant never clears even after very long flushing, while its residual is normal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone in a North Battleford area system. Crews flushed the hydrant on three visits with the same result and then sampled the main on both sides of the hydrant branch.

evidence.label: Main samples upstream and downstream of the hydrant branch are clear on all visits.
The hydrant itself drains slowly and its barrel holds rusty water between uses.
Removing the hydrant bonnet in an inspection finds heavy internal corrosion and a partly blocked drain.
After the hydrant is rebuilt, its first draw samples clear like the main.
Zone customer taps near the hydrant never reported discolouration.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The zone main has an endless sediment source no flushing can clear
Flushing crews are stirring the main worse with every visit
The hydrant itself, not the zone main, is producing the dirty samples that made the zone look unflushable
The treatment plant sends rusty water to this zone only

inference.explanation: Main samples on both sides are clear, customers are unaffected, the hydrant internals are found corroded with a blocked drain, and rebuilding it cures the sample. An endless main source would appear in main samples and at customer taps.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Flush the zone monthly for a year to chase the turbidity
Report the zone as failing its flushing target
Add hydrant condition checks to the flushing programme so sample points are proven before zone conclusions are drawn

nextClue.explanation: Proving sample points first protects programme conclusions from equipment artifacts like this one.

clueText.nc-a: A year of flushing would keep stirring a hydrant barrel, not a main.
clueText.nc-b: Reporting failure would misstate a zone whose mains tested clear throughout.
clueText.nc-c: The next programme round records the zone clear at the rebuilt hydrant on the first visit.
